hook: The cloth merchant who first saw bacteria through lenses he made himself.

pages.x: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was born in Delft in 1632, the same month as Vermeer. He had little schooling and no Latin, and became a draper, selling cloth. He used magnifying glasses to check the quality of the threads.
He learned to make tiny glass bead lenses and built more than 500 little microscopes, brass plates with a single lens, that magnified up to 270 times.
pages.fx: They were far better than anyone else's. He kept his method secret, and for over a century no one could match him.

pages.x: In 1674 he looked at a drop of lake water and saw it swarming with tiny creatures he called "animalcules". He was the first person ever to see bacteria and single-celled life.
pages.fx: He discovered the world of microbes. Two centuries later, Pasteur showed that such germs cause disease.

pages.x: He scraped the white gunk from between his teeth and found more "little animals" living in his mouth than there were people in the Netherlands. An old man who had never cleaned his teeth had, he wrote, "an unbelievably great company" of them.

He described what he saw in about 300 letters to the Royal Society in London, written in Dutch. The scientists doubted him at first, then sent witnesses who confirmed it all, and made him a member. He was also among the first to see sperm cells, red blood cells and capillaries.
Famous visitors came to look through his lenses, among them Peter the Great of Russia in 1698. He kept working until his death in 1723, aged 90, still sending letters about his discoveries.
Van Leeuwenhoek opened up an invisible world. He is called the father of microbiology, and everything we know about germs and microscopic life began with his tiny lenses.
pts: First to see bacteria and single-celled life
Built the best microscopes of his age
